title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with synthetic media, a deepfake video call in which the caller presented himself as a sitting chief minister and an actor. The impersonation was the entry point, not the whole scheme. Once the victim accepted the face on the call as proof of who was speaking, the fraud moved through a chain of invented roles, a manager, then someone claiming to be a CBI officer, and through documents, a letter about allotted funds and identity proof said to belong to that officer. The failure sits at the point of first contact, where a WhatsApp video call was treated as sufficient evidence of a public official's identity.

Catching it would have required verifying the caller through a channel independent of the call itself. Nothing in the call, the letter or the identity proof came from a source separate from the people making the demands, so each element corroborated only the others. The payment requests, exchange charges, a fee to unlock a PIN, a fine, were also the kind of demand that a check against the actual office would have exposed, since the supposed giver of aid was also the one asking for money.

What is not established is who made the calls or whether they produced the deepfake. A case has been registered under the Information Technology Act, which is a complaint recorded, not a finding against any person.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A security guard in Bengaluru, Ratikanta Giri, aged 29, lost more than Rs 1.04 lakh after a WhatsApp video call used an AI deepfake of Tamil Nadu Chief Minister and actor C Joseph Vijay. On Sept 9, the caller claimed to be Vijay and offered Rs 11 lakh in financial aid. A supposed manager then said Rs 5 lakh was allotted and asked for fees, including Rs 5,000 for exchange charges and Rs 18,000 to unlock a PIN. Another person posing as a CBI officer demanded over Rs 50,000 as a fine. Giri paid through a digital payment app until a further Rs 50,000 demand made him stop and realize the fraud.

Giri contacted the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then Byappanahalli police. A case has been registered under the Information Technology Act. This was the first such deepfake case reported in the city. Police advised people not to believe such calls or make payments based on them. The fraudsters had also sent Giri a letter claiming Rs 5 lakh was allotted and identity proof said to belong to a CBI officer.
